title: The Rise of Three.js
transcript: Before 3.js, putting 3D in the browser was technically possible, but it was awkward, low-level, and out of reach of most ordinary web developers. So, how did one developer's Flash era side project become the defining tool for 3D on the modern web? That's the story of 3.js. Back in the late 2000s, if you wanted to make something interactive and fun on the web, you were probably making it with Flash. Flash was where creative coders thrived. It was also closed source, plugin dependent, and existed on borrowed time. One of those creative coders was Ricardo Cabello, better known as Mr. Doob. He'd been experimenting with and building a 3D engine in Flash/ActionScript called 3.as. And in 2009, he ported it to JavaScript. Just a year before the first 3.js release landed on GitHub. The timing was significant. Chrome had just launched in 2008. JavaScript was suddenly very fast, and a new browser graphics API called WebGL was coming. WebGL brought hardware-accelerated 3D to the open web, no plugin required. The first official spec landed in 2011, building on years of experiments led by Vladimir Vukićević at Mozilla. >> But, there was a catch. Low-level graphics APIs like WebGL are powerful but painful to use. It gives you total control, and it demands attribute, boilerplate math, and technical knowledge before you can make anything that looks interesting. Just look at the code needed to generate and animate this single triangle. That's a triangle. One triangle. 3.js exists to hide all of that. It wraps the low-level complexity in concepts that you actually want to think about. Scenes, cameras, and meshes, lights, materials. Instead of fighting the GPU, you get to think like a designer, an animator, or a creative coder like me. >> The first version of three.js appeared on GitHub. And here's the decision that made everything else possible. Mr. Doob didn't hardwire it to one graphics back end. The renderer was modular from day one. >> That choice paid off almost immediately. When WebGL became practical across browsers in 2011, contributor Paul Brunt dropped a WebGL renderer without rewriting the library. The same flexibility would pay off again more than a decade later when three.js moved into the WebGPU era. >> The philosophy was simple and kind of genius. Abstract away the awkward parts, keep the API approachable, support multiple render targets, and allow people to get something on screen fast. Then came the thing that turns a cool side project into an unstoppable project, contributors. >> A wave of developers, artists, educators, and graphics nerds started shaping the library. Eugene 87, AlteredQualia, West Langley, Sunag, and many others whose names you'll see on almost every release. >> Suddenly, three.js was everywhere. Chrome experiments, interactive music videos, generative art toys, portfolio sites with transitions that were so good they felt illegal. >> At some point, it stopped being a library and evolved into a full-blown ecosystem. Official docs, a massive collection of examples, the three.js editor, a forum, a Discord, courses, starter kits, and thousands of community experiments. >> It's this ecosystem that lit the fire that led me to start Robot Bobby. One reason three.js spread the way it did isn't just the API, it's the culture around the examples. >> The examples are teaching tools. You can open up a demo, read the code, change a few values, pull a few levers, and learn how it works just by breaking it and fixing it. That's how I learned. And that's how a lot of self-taught 3.js developers learn, too. It's such a great idea that here's a thing that works, now go mess with it is a better teacher than a dry reference manual, and it's one of the reasons the community grew the way it did. It makes 3.js especially accessible to self-taught artists and developers like me. And now the story enters a new chapter with WebGPU. 3.js now ships with WebGL and WebGPU builds, which because the library sits on a wonderfully flexible render architecture, the new WebGPU API can be embraced and included without big disruptions. At the time I record this, the project has grown into a massive public open-source effort with thousands of contributors on GitHub and a global user base. And maybe the most important part of the story is that this was never a technical project. It was also a philosophical one, a push toward a more open, more accessible creative web. To quote Mr. Doob on X, "Money was never the goal. I hated relying on Adobe Flash so much that I felt I had to create a free option for the HTML5 WebGL world. It has not been easy, and I've had to sacrifice a few things in my personal life, but I think it has been worth it." Thanks to a large global community, 3.js has grown from one creator's experiments with math and graphics on the open web to the defining tool for real-time 3D on the internet.
